messages.content:
You are an independent classifier in a blinded experiment about a book of
biblical symbolism. The consensus responses below were produced without access
to the book. Compare them with the book's entry.

TERM
Remnant

BLIND CONSENSUS RESPONSES
RESPONSE A
{
  "primary_meaning": "In mainstream Christian teaching, the 'remnant' symbolizes the faithful minority of God's people whom He graciously preserves through judgment, exile, or widespread apostasy, guaranteeing the continuity of His covenant purposes. The remnant is understood as both a sign of judgment (only a small portion survives) and a sign of hope and grace (God does not utterly destroy His people but keeps a seed alive through whom salvation history continues). In New Testament interpretation, especially in Paul, the remnant becomes the believing minority 'chosen by grace,' demonstrating that God's promises have not failed even when the majority rejects them.",
  "primary_basis": [
    "Isaiah 10:20-22 (a remnant of Israel/Jacob will return to the mighty God)",
    "Isaiah 1:9 (unless the LORD had left us a few survivors, we would have been like Sodom)",
    "Isaiah 6:13 (the holy seed is the stump that remains)",
    "1 Kings 19:18 (the 7,000 in Israel who have not bowed the knee to Baal)",
    "Romans 11:1-5 (Paul cites Elijah: 'so too at the present time there is a remnant, chosen by grace')",
    "Romans 9:27-29 (quoting Isaiah: 'only a remnant will be saved')",
    "Genesis 45:7 (God sent Joseph 'to preserve for you a remnant on earth')",
    "Zephaniah 3:12-13 (a people humble and lowly left in the midst of Israel)",
    "Micah 2:12; 4:6-7; 5:7-8 (gathering of the remnant of Jacob)",
    "Jeremiah 23:3; 31:7 (God will gather the remnant of His flock)",
    "Ezra 9:8 (a remnant left as a peg in God's holy place)",
    "Amos 5:15 (perhaps the LORD will be gracious to the remnant of Joseph)",
    "Zechariah 8:11-12 (blessing on the remnant of the people)"
  ],
  "alternatives": [
    {
      "meaning": "Remnant primarily as a word of judgment rather than hope: in some prophetic contexts (especially Amos and parts of Isaiah), 'only a remnant' underscores the severity of destruction—so little survives that it emphasizes near-total loss rather than comfort. Critical scholarship often distinguishes this negative usage from the later positive 'remnant of hope' theology.",
      "basis": [
        "Amos 3:12 (as a shepherd rescues two legs or a piece of an ear)",
        "Isaiah 6:11-13 (devastation until the land is utterly forsaken)",
        "Isaiah 10:22 ('only a remnant will return; destruction is decreed')"
      ],
      "prominence": "common"
    },
    {
      "meaning": "Dispensationalist/futurist reading: the remnant refers specifically to a future believing Jewish remnant preserved and converted during the end times (the tribulation), distinct from the church, fulfilling promises of Israel's national restoration.",
      "basis": [
        "Zechariah 13:8-9 (a third refined through fire)",
        "Romans 11:25-27 ('all Israel will be saved')",
        "Revelation 7:1-8 (the 144,000 sealed from the tribes of Israel)",
        "Revelation 12:17 (the rest/remnant of the woman's offspring)"
      ],
      "prominence": "common"
    },
    {
      "meaning": "Seventh-day Adventist reading: the 'remnant' is an identifiable end-time remnant church characterized by keeping the commandments of God (including the Sabbath) and possessing 'the testimony of Jesus' (understood as the Spirit of Prophecy), which Adventists apply to their own movement.",
      "basis": [
        "Revelation 12:17 (KJV: 'the remnant of her seed, which keep the commandments of God, and have the testimony of Jesus Christ')",
        "Revelation 14:12"
      ],
      "prominence": "minority"
    },
    {
      "meaning": "Reformed/covenantal-election reading: the remnant is essentially identified with the elect—the true, invisible people of God within the visible community in every age—so 'remnant' becomes a theological synonym for God's sovereign election by grace and continuity between Israel and the church.",
      "basis": [
        "Romans 9:6-8 ('not all who are descended from Israel belong to Israel')",
        "Romans 11:5-7 (a remnant chosen by grace; 'the elect obtained it')",
        "Galatians 6:16 ('the Israel of God')"
      ],
      "prominence": "common"
    },
    {
      "meaning": "Ethical/devotional application: the remnant as a model for the faithful minority in any era—Christians called to remain faithful amid cultural decline or persecution ('remnant theology' as a posture of the church in a hostile society). This is an extension of the primary meaning rather than a rival exegesis.",
      "basis": [
        "1 Kings 19:18 applied typologically",
        "Zephaniah 3:12-13",
        "Matthew 7:13-14 (the few who find the narrow way, often linked thematically)"
      ],
      "prominence": "common"
    }
  ],
  "has_settled_consensus": true,
  "confidence": "high",
  "notes": "The remnant motif is one of the most stable and well-documented themes in biblical theology, traced from Genesis (Noah, Joseph) through the prophets (especially Isaiah, where the name Shear-jashub, 'a remnant shall return,' embodies the theme) to Paul's argument in Romans 9-11. The broad consensus—faithful minority preserved by God's grace through judgment, securing the continuity of His redemptive plan—is shared across Catholic, Orthodox, Protestant, and critical-scholarly traditions. Disagreement is not over this core meaning but over its referent and application: whether the present remnant is the church, a future Jewish remnant, a specific denomination (the Adventist claim), or simply the elect. Scholarly debate also concerns whether individual prophetic texts use the motif as threat or promise, but both poles are recognized within the consensus framework."
}

RESPONSE B
{

  "primary_basis": [
    "Isaiah 10:20-22",
    "Jeremiah 23:3",
    "Micah 2:12",
    "Romans 9:27",
    "Romans 11:4-5"
  ],

      "basis": [
        "Zechariah 13:8-9",
        "Romans 11:25-27",
        "Revelation 7:4-8"
      ],
      "prominence": "common"
    },
    {
      "meaning": "The literal historical survivors of the Babylonian exile who returned to Judah, viewed strictly in their immediate historical context rather than as an ongoing spiritual type.",
      "basis": [
        "Ezra 9:8",
        "Haggai 1:12",
        "Nehemiah 1:2"
      ],
      "prominence": "common"
    },
    {
      "meaning": "A specific end-time denomination or movement (e.g., in Seventh-day Adventist theology) that faithfully keeps God's commandments and possesses the spirit of prophecy.",
      "basis": [
        "Revelation 12:17",
        "Revelation 14:12"
      ],
      "prominence": "minority"
    }
  ],
  "has_settled_consensus": true,
  "confidence": "high",
  "notes": "While the fundamental theological concept of a faithful surviving minority chosen by grace is universally agreed upon across mainstream traditions, there is significant debate over its eschatological application, particularly regarding the distinction between the Church and national Israel in dispensational versus covenant theology."
}

RESPONSE C
{
  "primary_meaning": "The “remnant” most commonly symbolizes the surviving and often faithful portion of God’s covenant people whom God preserves through judgment, exile, apostasy, or calamity and from whom the community is renewed or restored.",
  "primary_basis": [
    "Isaiah 10:20–22 — a remnant of Israel returns and relies faithfully on the Lord.",
    "Isaiah 11:11–16 — God gathers the remnant of his people from dispersion.",
    "Isaiah 37:31–32 — the surviving remnant of Judah takes root and bears fruit.",
    "Micah 2:12; 5:7–8 — the remnant of Israel is gathered and preserved among the nations.",
    "Zephaniah 3:12–13 — a humble, purified remnant trusts in the Lord.",
    "Ezra 9:8, 13–15 — the postexilic community is described as a remnant spared by God.",
    "Romans 9:27–29 — Paul applies Isaiah’s remnant language to the portion of Israel that is saved.",
    "Romans 11:1–5 — Paul speaks of a remnant chosen by grace, using Elijah’s faithful minority as a pattern.",
    "1 Kings 19:18 — God preserves seven thousand in Israel who have not worshiped Baal."
  ],
  "alternatives": [
    {
      "meaning": "A historically surviving population after war, exile, plague, or judgment, without necessarily implying exceptional faithfulness or spiritual purity.",
      "basis": [
        "2 Kings 19:30–31",
        "2 Chronicles 34:21",
        "Jeremiah 42:2",
        "Ezekiel 5:3"
      ],
      "prominence": "common"
    },
    {
      "meaning": "The preserved Jewish people or faithful portion of Israel, especially in relation to Israel’s continuing election and anticipated restoration.",
      "basis": [
        "Isaiah 11:11–16",
        "Jeremiah 23:3",
        "Romans 9:27–29",
        "Romans 11:1–7, 25–29"
      ],
      "prominence": "common"
    },
    {
      "meaning": "A faithful minority within the visible church during periods of widespread apostasy, corruption, or persecution.",
      "basis": [
        "1 Kings 19:18 as a typological pattern",
        "Romans 11:2–5",
        "Revelation 2–3"
      ],
      "prominence": "common"
    },
    {
      "meaning": "A distinct end-time body of believers characterized by obedience to God’s commandments and testimony to Jesus; some traditions identify this with a particular denomination or movement.",
      "basis": [
        "Revelation 12:17, especially translations using “remnant”",
        "Revelation 14:12"
      ],
      "prominence": "minority"
    },
    {
      "meaning": "The postexilic Judean community or returned exiles specifically, rather than a transhistorical spiritual category.",
      "basis": [
        "Ezra 9:8, 13–15",
        "Nehemiah 1:3",
        "Haggai 1:12, 14"
      ],
      "prominence": "common"
    }
  ],
  "has_settled_consensus": true,
  "confidence": "high",
  "notes": "There is broad consensus on the core idea of a people preserved by God through crisis or judgment. Interpretation is less settled concerning the remnant’s precise identity, whether it is necessarily faithful, and whether the term refers primarily to Israel, the church, a historical group of survivors, or an end-time community."
}

RESPONSE D
{
  "primary_meaning": "A small, faithful core of God's people preserved by divine grace after judgment, disaster, exile, or widespread apostasy",
  "primary_basis": [
    "Isaiah 10:20-22",

      "basis": [

        "Nehemiah 1:3"
      ],
      "prominence": "common"
    },
    {
      "meaning": "End-time or eschatological pure church / faithful believers remaining amid final apostasy",
      "basis": [
        "Revelation 12:17",
        "applications of OT remnant texts to the church"
      ],
      "prominence": "common"
    },
    {
      "meaning": "Ethnic/national Israel as a distinct remnant preserved separately from the church",
      "basis": [
        "Romans 11:1-5, 25-26",
        "Isaiah remnant prophecies read dispensationally"
      ],
      "prominence": "minority"
    }
  ],
  "has_settled_consensus": true,
  "confidence": "high",
  "notes": "Standard Christian biblical interpretation, drawing from OT prophetic usage and NT Pauline application, consistently treats 'remnant' as the divinely preserved faithful minority rather than mere numerical remainder; secondary literal or eschatological nuances exist but do not displace the core symbolic sense."
}

BOOK ENTRY
The faithful few preserved and gathered from what remains — like gleanings left at the field’s edge and gold separated from dross.

BOOK'S COMMON-VIEW NOTE, IF PRESENT
(none)

SCRIPTURE REFERENCES PRINTED WITH THE ENTRY
(Ruth 2; 1 Kgs 19:18; Zech 13:8-9; Rom 11:5) · see The Remnant, ch. 15

CLASSIFY THE RELATIONSHIP

First reduce both readings to their minimum core identifications. Do not let
extra detail create an artificial disagreement.

- MATCH: the core identifications are equivalent. Differences are merely
  wording or immaterial detail.
- REFINED: the book preserves the consensus's general referent or category but
  materially changes its extension, boundary, conditions, or precision. A
  narrowing may reject some cases the broader consensus admits; a broadening
  may admit cases it excludes. This is real disagreement at the boundary, but
  not replacement of the central referent.
- DIVERGENT: the cores materially contradict. Both claims cannot be true of the
  same referent in the same context and sense; accepting the book requires
  rejecting or replacing the consensus identification. A source and its
  product remain different referents when the book explicitly denies their
  identity, even if they are causally related.
- NOVEL: no recognizable consensus or listed alternative covers the book's
  core identification. Novelty is absence from consensus, not contradiction.

Use `core_relation` to expose the relationship at the center and
`extension_relation` to expose disagreement over the cases covered. A REFINED
verdict must state what cases the book adds, excludes, or reclassifies. A
DIVERGENT verdict must identify a replaced referent or material contradiction,
not merely a narrower boundary.

Treat the two axes independently. A core-divergent reading may still retain
some cases covered by the consensus while rejecting its central identification;
therefore DIVERGENT does not require disjoint extensions. Conversely, a
narrowed extension is REFINED only when the consensus's central referent or
category remains intact.

Also judge whether the citations printed with the glossary entry alone provide
strong, partial, or insufficient support. Do not yet decide whether a divergent
full chapter is persuasive; that is a separate stage.
